questions.q: What is an Availability Zone (AZ), in the physical terms this lesson describes?
options: A single server rack inside one datacenter
A marketing label with no real physical separation behind it
One or more physically separate datacenters within a region, each with independent power, cooling, and network, linked to other AZs by low-latency connections
A backup copy of a region located on a different continent
questions.explain: An Availability Zone is one or more datacenters physically separated from the datacenters backing other AZs in the same region, each with its own independent power, cooling, and network path, connected by high-bandwidth, low-latency private links.

questions.q: A workload is deployed across three Availability Zones in one region and nowhere else. What does this architecture actually protect against?
options: The loss of a single datacenter's power, cooling, or local network
A region-wide power grid failure or natural disaster affecting the whole region
A regulatory requirement to keep data in a second country
Nothing — multi-AZ provides no resilience at all
questions.explain: Multi-AZ deployment protects against losing an entire datacenter, since AZs have independent power/cooling/network. It assumes the region itself stays up and does not protect against a region-wide event.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say multi-AZ high availability (HA) is not the same thing as disaster recovery (DR)?
options: Because HA and DR are simply two marketing terms for the identical architecture
Because DR requires more servers in the same datacenter than HA does
Because HA only applies to AWS and DR only applies to Azure
Because HA assumes the region stays up and only protects against datacenter-level failure, while DR requires surviving a region-wide failure, which only a second region provides
questions.explain: Multi-AZ HA assumes the region itself stays up; it is a different failure domain than a region-wide disaster. True DR requires a second region, since every AZ in a single region can still share exposure to a region-wide event.

questions.q: In the Terraform aws_autoscaling_group example in this lesson, what does vpc_zone_identifier listing three different AZ subnets actually accomplish?
options: It deploys the Auto Scaling Group into three separate regions
It spreads instances across three Availability Zones within one region, implementing multi-AZ high availability — but with no capacity anywhere outside that region
It automatically fails the application over to a second region if the first one goes down
It has no effect on resilience and only controls instance pricing
questions.explain: Listing subnets from three different AZs spreads the Auto Scaling Group across those AZs, which is exactly how multi-AZ HA is implemented in real infrastructure — but every one of those AZs is still inside a single region.

questions.q: What is the smallest failure domain described in this lesson's hierarchy?
options: An entire cloud provider's global footprint
A Region
An individual datacenter, with its own power feed, cooling plant, and network uplinks
An Availability Zone
questions.explain: A datacenter — one physical building with its own power, cooling, and network uplinks — is the smallest failure domain in the hierarchy; Availability Zones group datacenters, and Regions group Availability Zones.
